lessons.title: Thermodynamic Cycles
lessons.objective: Apply the Otto and Diesel cycles to aero piston engine operation: relate the four strokes to crankshaft and piston movement, read the ideal and practical Otto pressure-volume diagram, explain valve lead, lag and overlap, and distinguish the Diesel cycle by how it adds heat and starts combustion - while keeping ideal teaching diagrams separate from manufacturer timing and measured pressure data.
lessons.completionCriteria: Describe the four events of a four-stroke cycle in order and why it takes 720 crankshaft degrees, and state how a two-stroke cycle completes the same events in one revolution; label the four processes of the ideal Otto cycle on a pressure-volume diagram and give two reasons the practical diagram differs; explain valve lead, lag and overlap and why overlap helps rather than harms; and state how the Diesel cycle differs from the Otto cycle in heat addition and ignition - without treating an illustrative diagram as measured engine data.

steps.title: What cycle means
steps.prompt: An operating cycle describes how an engine repeats the events needed to turn fuel energy into shaft rotation. Before looking at the four named cycles, predict which features belong to the cycle itself and which belong to another classification, such as cylinder layout or cooling method.
steps.note: Documented classification frame from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48, cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 20-23.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short prediction establishes the classification boundary more clearly than a visual.

steps.title: Four-stroke sequence
steps.prompt: Use the crank-angle scrubber to move through intake, compression, power and exhaust. Watch one complete cycle require two crankshaft revolutions while the piston completes four strokes.
steps.note: Documented sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The planned animation will show phase, piston direction and ideal valve state only; it will not display invented pressure, temperature or flow values.

mediaPlan.rationale: Scrubbing a 720-degree state makes the repeated sequence and two-revolution relationship observable.

steps.title: Intake pose
steps.prompt: At 90 degrees, predict the piston's direction and which ideal-cycle valve should be open. Reveal the GTSIO-520-H teaching-cylinder pose, then separate what the model proves geometrically from what its coloured gas cue only illustrates.
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. The mechanism pose is profile-checked; valve and gas cues remain an ideal teaching profile, not certified GTSIO-520-H timing or CFD.

mediaPlan.rationale: The existing operating-cylinder model directly shows the crank, rod and piston relationship at a chosen angle.

steps.title: Power pose
steps.prompt: At 450 degrees the piston is travelling the same direction as at 90 degrees, yet compression has come and gone in between. Compare the two poses: which mechanical motion repeats, and which cycle event has changed?
steps.note: Documented four-stroke sequence from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48. In the shared 720-degree teaching profile 0-180 is intake, 180-360 compression, 360-540 power and 540-720 exhaust, so 450 degrees is mid-power stroke; the profile distinguishes the second crankshaft revolution from the first.

mediaPlan.rationale: A paired pose comparison (both poses descending) shows why piston direction alone does not identify the stroke.

steps.title: Ideal Otto cycle
steps.prompt: A pressure-volume (PV) diagram plots the cylinder's pressure against its volume through one cycle. Step through the ideal Otto cycle and watch the piston beside it. Which two processes hold the volume constant, and which two have no heat exchange?
steps.note: Neither FAA-H-8083-32B nor EASA Module 16 covers pressure-volume diagram theory (both searched 29 September 2026). Ideal Otto processes (two adiabatic, two constant-volume) are from the instructor's course deck, slides 56 and 58 (tier 4), and the Wikipedia Otto cycle article (tier 5, CC BY-SA 4.0, accessed 29 September 2026). The curves are schematic ideal-gas shapes, not data for any engine. Cross-checked against MIT Unified Engineering, 'Thermodynamics and Propulsion' section 3.5 (isentropic compression and expansion; constant-volume combustion and heat rejection; tier 4 textbook-grade source) and NASA Glenn's Otto cycle page (combustion at constant volume; no heat exchange during the compression and power strokes).

mediaPlan.rationale: Stepping a marker around the loop while the piston moves shows how each process links to a stroke.

steps.title: Why constant volume?
steps.prompt: The ideal cycle treats combustion as instant heat addition while the piston sits at top dead centre, so the volume cannot change and the pressure jumps straight up. Real burning takes time, which is why the spark fires before TDC and cylinder pressure peaks a little after it. The ideal loop also leaves out the pumping done on the intake and exhaust strokes.
steps.note: Ideal-cycle assumptions from the course deck, slide 56 (tier 4), and Wikipedia Otto cycle (tier 5). Spark before TDC and the pressure peak after TDC are documented in FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 48 and 51.

mediaPlan.rationale: The constant-volume idea is stated once, directly after the diagram that shows it.

steps.title: Ideal versus practical
steps.prompt: Switch between the ideal and practical diagrams. Find two differences in shape, then link each to a physical cause: burning takes time, heat is lost to the cylinder walls, and valves open early and close late.
steps.note: FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 48 and 51 (Figure 1-39) documents the actual cylinder-pressure diagram and its peak after top center. The list of causes follows the course deck, slides 57-58 (tier 4). The practical curve is an illustrative rounding of the ideal loop, not measured data. MIT section 3.5 notes the actual cycle lacks the sharp transitions between processes that the ideal cycle has, and NASA Glenn notes the real cycle's enclosed area (work) is always less than the ideal value.

mediaPlan.rationale: Overlaying the ideal loop as a dashed line makes each departure from the ideal visible.

steps.title: Valve lead, lag and overlap
steps.prompt: Move the crank through the FAA example timing chart. Find where each valve opens and closes relative to TDC and BDC, and locate the interval around TDC when both valves are open.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 47, Figure 1-37 (example valve timing chart) and its text: valve events vary considerably in different engines, and the manufacturer's recommendations must be followed. The chart values are an FAA example, not GTSIO-520-H timing; the GTSIO-520 manual searched here gives no valve timing figures. The instructor accepted the FAA example chart for this lesson (29 September 2026).

mediaPlan.rationale: A crank-angle marker over a two-revolution timeline shows valve state and overlap at any angle.

steps.title: Why overlap helps
steps.prompt: The intake valve opens before TDC on the exhaust stroke (valve lead), and the exhaust valve closes after TDC (valve lag). The overlap cools the cylinder internally with cool incoming charge, draws in more mixture and helps scavenge burnt gas. It works because moving gas has momentum: the outgoing exhaust leaves the cylinder at low pressure, which speeds the fresh charge in. Timing is limited, though - open the intake too early and hot gas can flash back; close it too late and charge can be pushed back out.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 47-48 (valve lead, valve lag, valve overlap, scavenging effect and the limits on early opening and late closing).

mediaPlan.rationale: The merits and limits of lead and lag follow the diagram that defines them.

steps.title: Other cycles
steps.prompt: The four-stroke Otto cycle spreads intake, compression, power and exhaust over four strokes and two crankshaft revolutions. A two-stroke engine completes the same operating cycle in one revolution by combining intake and exhaust in the same stroke. A rotary engine has no reciprocating piston at all: a three-sided rotor turns inside an elliptical housing. Follow either link for the detail; neither is needed to continue.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 46-48, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 19-23. The two-stroke and rotary cycles are standalone deep-dive lessons (instructor decision, 29 September 2026); this step keeps the outcome 'interrelate the 4 and 2 stroke Otto cycle' in the main flow.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short orienting step; the detail and visuals sit in the linked deep dives.

steps.title: Diesel versus Otto
steps.prompt: Compare the two ideal cycles. Both start with the same compression, so predict which one process differs before you toggle, and what that means for how the fuel burns. Then raise the compression ratio and notice how each loop changes.
steps.note: Diesel cycle description documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23; EASA PDF p. 210 notes the diesel compression ratio is far greater than a gasoline engine's. The constant-pressure heat-addition process is from the course deck, slide 76 (tier 4), and Wikipedia Diesel cycle (tier 5, CC BY-SA 4.0, accessed 29 September 2026). Neither FAA-H-8083-32B nor EASA Module 16 covers pressure-volume diagram theory (both searched 29 September 2026). Curves are schematic. Cross-checked against MIT section 3.6: compression ignition, fuel sprayed in once compression is complete, and a higher compression ratio is possible because only air is compressed with no risk of auto-ignition.

mediaPlan.rationale: Overlaying the two loops isolates the single process that differs: constant-volume versus constant-pressure heat addition.

steps.title: Diesel combustion
steps.prompt: A diesel-cycle engine first compresses air alone. Near maximum pressure fuel is sprayed in, and the high pressure and temperature make it burn without a spark; the rising pressure drives the piston down. Because the fuel burns as it is injected, the ideal diesel cycle adds heat at roughly constant pressure while the piston moves away from TDC. 'Diesel' names the ignition strategy - two-stroke and four-stroke diesels both exist.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23. Constant-pressure heat addition from the course deck, slide 76 (tier 4). Replaces the earlier single 'Diesel ignition' step; the spark-versus-compression comparison now lives in lesson 5. Cross-checked against MIT section 3.6 (fuel sprayed into the cylinder when compression is complete; ignition without a spark).

mediaPlan.rationale: The combustion sequence is short and follows the diagram just studied.

steps.title: Diesel in aviation
steps.prompt: Diesel-cycle engines can burn Jet A, but regulators raised specific concerns when they returned to small aeroplanes. Turbine fuel must be accommodated in fuel systems designed for gasoline. A conventional diesel vibrates badly if one cylinder stops firing, which can damage the airframe and propeller. High internal pressures mean cylinder parts could be shed in a failure. The engine needs FADEC control with its own limits and indications. Add heavier construction, complex fuel injection, long cold-weather cranking and the risk of misfuelling.
steps.note: Aero-specific concerns are from the FAA's proposed special conditions for the Piper PA-28-236 with an SMA SR305-230 diesel engine (Federal Register vol. 71 no. 114, 14 June 2006): turbine fuel in gasoline-designed systems, vibration and failure modes with a cylinder inoperative, high-energy fragments from high internal pressures, FADEC control, and limitations and indications. The FAA states these concerns are not universally applicable to all diesel engines. Heavier construction, complex injection and cold cranking are from the course deck, slide 78 (tier 4); misfuelling from EASA Module 16, PDF p. 228. The FAA and EASA handbook texts contain no limitations list, so per the instructor's decision (29 September 2026) this step uses the FAA notice, the deck and common engineering sense.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short list of concerns needs no visual.

steps.title: Choose the evidence
steps.prompt: A diagram can establish event order and mechanical relationships. It cannot, by appearance alone, establish a real engine's valve timing, cylinder pressure, gas temperature or efficiency. Those claims need an applicable manual or a validated analytical model.
steps.note: Documented evidence boundary carried forward from the platform architecture. Manufacturer-specific timing remains controlled by the applicable engine data; FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, explicitly directs ignition timing to the engine manufacturer's recommendation.

mediaPlan.rationale: This is an evidence-literacy synthesis step.

lessons.title: Classification
lessons.objective: Classify a piston engine on separate axes - cylinder arrangement (inline, V-type, radial, horizontally opposed) and ignition method (spark or compression) - and explain how arrangement influences frontal area, cooling access, crankshaft/rod layout and installation without turning typical traits into universal rules.
lessons.completionCriteria: Correctly identify the four conventional arrangements from a plan/front view and explain at least one source-backed installation consequence for each, identify the GTSIO-520-H as a six-cylinder horizontally opposed engine, and state what initiates combustion in spark-ignition and compression-ignition engines.

steps.title: One new axis
steps.prompt: Operating cycle and cylinder arrangement answer different questions. A four-stroke engine may be inline, V-type, radial or opposed. Predict which arrangement would give the narrowest frontal outline and which would place cylinders around a central crankcase.
steps.note: Documented classification from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24-25, cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 23-25.

mediaPlan.rationale: The prompt activates spatial predictions before the visual comparison.

steps.title: Inline bank
steps.prompt: Identify the single straight bank and the crankshaft above or below it. Compare upright and inverted installations, and notice the small frontal area of the arrangement.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24. Use an FAA source figure or an accuracy-checked redraw; retain the upright/inverted distinction.

mediaPlan.rationale: An accuracy-checked schematic communicates the single-bank geometry without implying a specific engine.

steps.title: V-type banks
steps.prompt: Find the two inline banks sharing one crankshaft. Use the bank angle and common crankshaft to distinguish a V engine from two separate inline engines.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 25. The handbook describes two inline banks, generally set 60 degrees apart; the lesson should avoid implying that every V engine uses the same angle or cylinder count.

mediaPlan.rationale: The defining relationship is geometric and reads best in a controlled front-view schematic.

steps.title: Radial rows
steps.prompt: Trace one row of cylinders around the central crankcase. Then compare a single row with multiple staggered rows and identify why the front view, not a side silhouette alone, is needed to recognise the arrangement.
steps.alt: FAA single-row and double-row radial engine examples
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 25-27. Use FAA Figures 1-2 and 1-3 as the first-choice visual source.

mediaPlan.rationale: The handbook figures already show the single-row and double-row geometry accurately.

steps.title: Opposed engine
steps.prompt: Orbit the six-cylinder GTSIO-520-H and identify the two banks directly opposite one another with the crankshaft between them. Predict which view makes the opposed layout most obvious before revealing the model.
steps.note: Documented general arrangement from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24-25. The GTSIO-520 overhaul manual identifies the basic engine as six-cylinder, horizontally opposed (PDF p. 13). The current whole-engine mesh is a teaching reconstruction and must retain its modelling-status disclosure.

mediaPlan.rationale: Free orbit makes the two opposed banks and central crankshaft spatially obvious.

steps.title: Arrangement compare
steps.prompt: Switch among inline, V-type, radial and opposed outlines. Rotate the same notional engine axis and compare bank count, cylinder direction and frontal outline without changing the operating cycle.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24-25, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 23-25. The comparator will use schematic silhouettes, not claim exact dimensions for a real engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: A single controlled comparator prevents scale and viewpoint changes from obscuring the geometry difference.

steps.title: Configuration, not verdict
steps.prompt: Arrangement affects packaging, cooling paths, balance and maintenance access, but it does not decide the whole engine. Cooling, ignition, aspiration, materials and installation still matter. Treat each stated advantage or limitation as typical and source-bounded, not universal.
steps.note: Documented synthesis of the FAA and EASA configuration sections. This boundary prevents the lesson from turning a layout label into an unsupported claim about every engine of that type.

mediaPlan.rationale: The closing distinction is conceptual.

steps.title: Ignition compare
steps.prompt: Predict what supplies the initiating energy in a spark-ignition engine and in a compression-ignition engine, then toggle between them. Scrub through the end of compression and observe what enters the cylinder, when fuel is present, and what initiates combustion in each case.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 47-48, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23. The diesel cycle itself is taught in lesson 4; this step only contrasts the trigger. The animation is qualitative and assigns no unsourced compression ratios, injection pressures or temperatures.

mediaPlan.rationale: A controlled toggle keeps piston position constant while changing only the ignition mechanism.

steps.title: Name all three
steps.prompt: Operating cycle, cylinder arrangement and ignition method are separate classifications. A diesel engine can use a two-stroke or four-stroke cycle, and a four-stroke engine can use spark ignition or compression ignition. Name all three when describing an engine - the GTSIO-520-H, for example, is a four-stroke, six-cylinder horizontally opposed, spark-ignition engine.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, which notes both two-stroke and four-stroke diesel cycles. The GTSIO-520-H's spark ignition follows from the overhaul manual's magneto and spark-plug description (PDF pp. 15, 18-19); instructor to confirm this wording.

mediaPlan.rationale: A verbal classification check prevents a common category error.

lessons.title: Parts and Construction
lessons.objective: Name the major structural and power-section parts of a piston engine - crankcase sections, crankshaft, connecting rods, pistons, rings and pins, cylinders, bearings, propeller shaft and mounts - state what each does and what it is made of, and recognise how the GTSIO-520-H's construction differs from a direct-drive engine such as the IO-520.
lessons.completionCriteria: Name the parts of the power section in the order force passes through them, state one function and one material for the crankcase, crankshaft, piston and cylinder, give the difference between compression and oil control rings, and explain how the GTSIO-520-H's propeller drive differs from a direct-drive engine.

steps.title: The basic parts
steps.prompt: Every piston engine is built from the same core parts: a crankcase, cylinders, pistons, connecting rods, a crankshaft, and valves with their operating mechanism. Before opening them up, predict which part carries the whole engine's load and keeps the crankshaft in alignment.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 26 (major components of a reciprocating engine; the crankcase must be rigid enough to prevent misalignment of the crankshaft and its bearings).

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt frames the walk through the components.

steps.title: The crankcase
steps.prompt: The crankcase is the foundation. It holds the crankshaft bearings, supports the cylinders and carries the mounting lugs, so it must stay rigid under bending and vibration. It is normally cast or forged aluminium alloy. On the GTSIO-520-H, two aluminium alloy castings, left and right, are joined along the vertical centre plane.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 26-27, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 51, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Section III paragraph 3-1b (PDF p. 16). The whole-engine mesh is a teaching reconstruction and keeps its modelling-status disclosure.

mediaPlan.rationale: The whole-engine model shows the two crankcase halves with the cylinders on each side.

steps.title: Sections of the case
steps.prompt: Find the two crankcase halves, the accessory (rear) case and the oil sump. The nose section at the front houses the propeller shaft, or the reduction gears on a geared engine, while the rear section carries the magnetos, pumps, starter and alternator.
steps.alt: FAA exploded view of an opposed engine showing the crankcase halves, accessory case, oil sump, crankshaft, camshaft, cylinder and accessories
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 26-28 (nose section, accessory section, Figure 1-6). Sump construction differs by engine: the IO-520 manual notes cast or stamped aluminium sumps.

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA exploded view names every major case section and accessory in one labelled figure.

steps.title: The crankshaft
steps.prompt: The crankshaft is the engine's backbone: a forged alloy steel shaft with a throw for each cylinder. A throw is two crank cheeks and a crankpin, and the journals turn in the main bearings. The crankpin is usually hollow, which saves weight and carries oil. The GTSIO-520-H's six-throw shaft has nitrided journals and crankpins, and counterweights that oscillate on pins to damp torsional vibration.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 29-30, EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 53-55, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Section III paragraph 3-1e (PDF pp. 16-17). The model shows one throw of the detailed operating cylinder.

mediaPlan.rationale: Spotlighting one crank throw on the operating-cylinder model shows cheeks, crankpin and journal in place.

steps.title: Connecting rods
steps.prompt: The connecting rod links the piston to the crankpin. It must stay rigid under load yet be light enough to limit inertia forces at each stroke end. Opposed and inline engines use plain rods, with a cap and two-piece bearing at the crankpin end and a bushing at the piston end. Rods go back in the same cylinder and position. The GTSIO-520-H uses I-beam rods with split bronze piston-pin bushings.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 30-32, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 66, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1f (PDF p. 17): I-beam rods, two identical precision inserts at the crankpin end, weight variation limited to 1/2 ounce in a bay.

mediaPlan.rationale: The rod, cap, bearing halves, bolts and small-end bushing are spotlighted together.

steps.title: Other rod types
steps.prompt: Radial engines use a master rod with articulated rods, and V engines use fork-and-blade rods. Match the four connecting-rod types in the figure - plain, fork-and-blade, master-and-articulated, and split-type - to the engine layouts that use them.
steps.alt: FAA diagram of connecting rod assemblies: solid master rod with articulated rod, fork-and-blade rod, plain rod and split-type master rod
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 30-32 (four types of connecting-rod assembly; Figure 1-11) and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 66.

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA figure shows all four rod assemblies side by side with their parts labelled.

steps.title: Piston and pin
steps.prompt: The piston is the moving wall of the combustion chamber: an aluminium alloy forging with ring grooves, heavy pin bosses and inner ribs that help oil carry heat away. The full-floating piston pin turns freely in both the piston and the rod, and soft aluminium end plugs stop it scoring the cylinder wall.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 33-34, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 63, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1g (PDF p. 17): aluminium alloy pistons with solid skirts, full-floating ground steel pins with forged-in aluminium plugs.

mediaPlan.rationale: The piston body, pin and end plugs are spotlighted with the cylinder ghosted around them.

steps.title: Piston rings
steps.prompt: Rings seal the combustion gas and control the oil. Compression rings, usually two, sit nearest the crown; oil control rings scrape surplus oil back to the crankcase. Most rings are gray cast iron, and chrome rings belong only with steel cylinder walls. This piston has two compression rings, a slotted oil-control ring and an oil scraper. The GTSIO-520 series has used a four-ring piston since 1975, and piston types must not be intermixed.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 34-35, EASA Module 16, PDF p. 65, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1g (PDF p. 17): four-ring piston since 1975, replacing the five-ring model; some pistons have a cast steel top-groove insert and the weight difference means they are not to be intermixed.

mediaPlan.rationale: The four rings are spotlighted so each can be named by its job.

steps.title: The cylinder
steps.prompt: Each cylinder is two parts: a light aluminium alloy head with deep cooling fins, and a steel barrel nitrided inside to resist wear. The head is heated and screwed onto the chilled barrel, so as they equalise they lock into a gastight shrink joint. The head also carries the valve seats and guides and the spark plug openings.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 35-36, EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 56-57, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1c (PDF p. 16): heads heated, seats and guides installed, then screwed and shrunk onto the steel barrel; 18 mm helical-coil spark plug inserts.

mediaPlan.rationale: The barrel and head are spotlighted as one assembly.

steps.title: Bearings
steps.prompt: Bearings support moving parts with little friction and carry radial loads, thrust loads, or both. Plain bearings of soft alloys serve the crankshaft, camshaft and connecting rods. Deep-groove ball bearings carry radial and thrust loads; straight roller bearings carry radial load only. The GTSIO-520-H's crankshaft rides in precision steel-backed, lead-alloy-lined main bearing inserts.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 43-44 (radial and thrust loads; plain, ball and roller bearings), and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, paragraph 3-1b (PDF p. 16).

mediaPlan.rationale: A short classification by load type needs no visual.

steps.title: Propeller shaft and reduction gears
steps.prompt: The propeller shaft is tapered, splined or flanged; on small direct-drive engines it is just an extension of the crankshaft. Powerful engines add reduction gears so the crankshaft can turn fast while the propeller turns slower, before its tip speed nears the speed of sound. Name the three common types in the figure. The GTSIO-520-H is geared: a quill shaft carries torque to a reduction gear that drives the flanged propeller shaft at 0.667:1.
steps.alt: FAA diagram of propeller reduction gears: spur planetary, bevel planetary, and spur and pinion
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 44-45, EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 67-70, and the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual (PDF pp. 16-17 for the quill shaft and reduction gear; PDF p. 152 for the 0.667:1 propeller drive ratio).

mediaPlan.rationale: The FAA figure shows the three reduction-gear arrangements with their parts named.

steps.title: Engine mounts
steps.prompt: The engine hangs from the airframe on an engine mount: a steel-tube structure with a ring that surrounds the engine near its point of balance. Dynafocal mounts angle their pads toward the engine's centre of gravity. Rubber-and-steel shock mounts let the engine move a little while metal snubbers limit extreme movement. Rubber ages, so hoses and controls must be able to flex.
steps.alt: Photograph of an engine mounting ring on a light aircraft firewall with four dynamic mount fittings
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 27 and 343-344 (mounting lugs, mount ring, dynafocal and shock mounts), and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 53 and 275-276 (rubber mounts, relative motion between engine and airframe).

mediaPlan.rationale: A photograph of a real mounting ring shows the fittings that hold the dynamic mounts.

steps.title: Direct or geared?
steps.prompt: Compare the GTSIO-520-H with the IO-520 part by part. Find what is identical and what differs. Which difference changes how the propeller is attached to the engine?
steps.note: GTSIO-520-H from its overhaul manual, Section III (PDF pp. 16-17) and Chapter C-3 (PDF p. 152). IO-520 from its overhaul manual, paragraphs 2-3 to 2-9. The IO-520 is a different engine, used for comparison only.

mediaPlan.rationale: A side-by-side table makes identical and differing construction obvious at a glance.

lessons.title: Two-stroke cycle
lessons.objective: Explain how a two-stroke engine completes the operating cycle in one crankshaft revolution by combining intake and exhaust in the same stroke, and where it is used in aircraft.
lessons.completionCriteria: State that a two-stroke cycle completes in one crankshaft revolution, name the functions that share a stroke, and give one advantage and one disadvantage compared with the four-stroke cycle.

steps.title: One revolution, one cycle
steps.prompt: A four-stroke engine needs two crankshaft revolutions for one cycle. A two-stroke engine needs only one upstroke and one downstroke, so it completes the operating cycle in a single revolution and every cylinder fires once per revolution. Predict how that is possible: what has to happen to the intake and exhaust functions?
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48: two upstroke-and-downstroke pairs are not needed; the cycle completes in one revolution and 'the intake and exhaust functions are accomplished during the same stroke'. That every cylinder fires once per revolution follows from one cycle per revolution.

mediaPlan.rationale: A prediction prompt frames the port-timing interactive that follows.

steps.title: Port timing
steps.prompt: Step through one crankshaft revolution of a two-stroke cycle. Observe how intake and exhaust functions share part of the same piston movement, rather than occupying four separate strokes.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48. The FAA text states that a two-stroke cycle completes in one crankshaft revolution and combines intake and exhaust functions during the same stroke.

mediaPlan.rationale: Port opening and closing are time relationships; a learner-controlled phase animation is clearer than a single still.

steps.title: Where two-strokes fly
steps.prompt: The two-stroke engine has re-emerged in ultra-light, light sport and many experimental aircraft. These engines can be air or water cooled and generally need a gear reduction housing between engine and propeller. The course's comparison lists a power stroke every revolution, light and simple construction (no valves) and compact size as advantages, against lower fuel efficiency, shorter time between overhauls, more emissions and poorer scavenging.
steps.note: Aircraft use, cooling and gear reduction documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48. The advantages and disadvantages list is the course deck, slides 65 and 67 (tier 4); it is not in the FAA or EASA text.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short comparison list needs no visual.

lessons.title: Rotary (Wankel) cycle
lessons.objective: Describe how a rotary engine produces the four cycle events in chambers around a three-sided rotor instead of in a reciprocating piston engine's cylinders.
lessons.completionCriteria: Describe the rotor and housing, name the four events that occur in the chambers, and give one advantage and one disadvantage of the rotary engine.

steps.title: A rotor instead of a piston
steps.prompt: A rotary (Wankel) engine has no reciprocating piston. A three-sided rotor turns inside an elliptical housing, and the four events of the cycle take place in the changing chambers between rotor and housing. These engines can have one rotor or several, can be air or water cooled, are used mostly in experimental and light aircraft, and have very low vibration.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 22-23.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short orientation before the source figure.

steps.title: Chambers around the rotor
steps.prompt: Trace how the three-sided rotor creates changing chambers for intake, compression, combustion/expansion and exhaust while producing rotary output.
steps.alt: EASA diagram showing intake, compression, power and exhaust chambers in a rotary engine
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 22-23. Use the source figure first. A short licensed or self-authored motion clip is optional only if the static chamber sequence proves insufficient in review.

mediaPlan.rationale: The EASA source already supplies the required rotor, housing and phase geometry; a generated technical image would add avoidable fidelity risk.

steps.title: Rotary trade-offs
steps.prompt: The course lists the strengths of the Wankel as very compact and light, few moving parts and so low vibration, and no valves. Against that come lower thermal efficiency from the shape of the combustion chamber, poor emissions control, faster apex-seal wear, higher fuel and oil consumption, and limited certification and support in aviation.
steps.note: Advantages and disadvantages are the course deck, slide 71 (tier 4); they are not in the FAA or EASA text.

mediaPlan.rationale: A short comparison list needs no visual.

lessons.parkedFor: Lesson 8 (Accessories & Drives) - magnetos and dual ignition. The spark-vs-compression comparison now lives in lesson 5 (Classification).
lessons.title: Ignition and timing (parked draft)
lessons.objective: Relate ignition timing to piston position and explain the GTSIO-520 dual-plug magneto arrangement at an introductory level without substituting a general lesson for applicable maintenance data.
lessons.completionCriteria: State why spark occurs before top dead centre in a four-stroke spark-ignition engine and describe the GTSIO-520 two-plug-per-cylinder arrangement without attempting an unsupervised timing procedure.

steps.title: Spark before TDC
steps.prompt: Move to the end of compression and inspect the piston near top dead centre. The general four-stroke source explains that the spark occurs before TDC so combustion can develop as the piston crosses the top. What would be wrong with treating this ideal pose as the exact timing value for every engine?
steps.note: Documented general principle from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48. The handbook gives a broad 20-35 degrees BTDC range across various engines and explicitly requires the manufacturer's setting. The 355-degree pose is illustrative, not GTSIO-520 timing data.

mediaPlan.rationale: The cylinder model shows piston position relative to TDC while the note enforces the timing evidence boundary.

steps.title: Dual ignition
steps.prompt: Follow the GTSIO-520 ignition paths from the left and right magnetos to the upper and lower spark plugs. Each cylinder has two plugs, and the two magnetos distribute high voltage to complementary plug positions.
steps.alt: Continental GTSIO-520 upper and lower spark-plug ignition wiring diagram
steps.credit: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Figure A4-43
steps.note: Documented from the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 15, 18-19 and 50. Use the manual wiring diagram as the visual; do not redraw or simplify cable destinations without checking every label and connection.

mediaPlan.rationale: The manufacturer diagram is the safest way to preserve actual plug and magneto routing.

steps.title: Manual controls timing
steps.prompt: The correct timing value and adjustment procedure belong to the applicable engine maintenance data. A general animation can explain why timing matters, but it cannot authorize a setting or maintenance action.
steps.note: Documented boundary from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 48, and the configuration-specific GTSIO-520 overhaul manual.

mediaPlan.rationale: This safety and applicability boundary should remain prominent text.

lessons.title: Cooling Methods
lessons.objective: Trace heat from the cylinder to the surrounding air in air-cooled, liquid-cooled and combined systems, identify the roles of fins, baffles, coolant, pump and radiator, and recognise why cooling condition and airflow path matter.
lessons.completionCriteria: Draw or explain the heat path for an air-cooled and liquid-cooled engine, identify two airflow-control features on an air-cooled installation, and state that the GTSIO-520 course engine is air cooled.

steps.title: Where heat goes
steps.prompt: Combustion releases more heat than the engine can convert to useful work. Predict the path that unwanted heat must take from the cylinder metal to the atmosphere in an air-cooled engine and in a liquid-cooled engine.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24 and 278-282, cross-checked against EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 23 and 201.

mediaPlan.rationale: The heat-path prediction prepares learners to interpret the system diagrams.

steps.title: Air-cooled path
steps.prompt: Trace heat from the cylinder wall and head into the fins, then into air directed through the cowling and baffles. Identify how added fin area supports convection.
steps.alt: FAA cylinder baffle and deflector airflow diagram
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 24 and 278-282. Use the FAA cylinder-head/fin and cowling/baffle figures as the primary image source.

mediaPlan.rationale: A labelled source schematic clearly establishes the directed airflow path around the cylinder.

steps.title: GTSIO cooling fins
steps.prompt: Inspect the GTSIO-520-H cylinder banks and locate the finned surfaces exposed to the installation airflow. Use the model to understand location and access, not to infer an exact heat-transfer rate.
steps.note: The GTSIO-520 overhaul manual identifies the basic engine as air cooled (PDF p. 13). The model is suitable for spatial inspection but is not a thermal simulation.

mediaPlan.rationale: The whole-engine model shows where the finned cylinders sit relative to the crankcase and installation airflow.

steps.title: Liquid-cooled path
steps.prompt: In a liquid-cooled engine, heat moves from the cylinder into coolant, then through tubing to a radiator in the airstream. A pump circulates the coolant. This adds coolant, radiator, pump and tubing mass, but it can support high power and closer control of component temperature.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 24, and EASA Module 16, PDF p. 23. The sources identify added system weight as the principal disadvantage and note that some light-aircraft engines combine air and liquid cooling.

mediaPlan.rationale: The system path is short enough to establish in text before a comparison graphic.

steps.title: Combined cooling
steps.prompt: Study an example in which liquid cools the cylinder heads while air cools the cylinder barrels. Follow each heat path separately rather than labelling the whole engine as only air cooled or only liquid cooled.
steps.alt: Rotax combined liquid-head and air-barrel cooling system diagram
steps.credit: EASA Module 16 course reference, Rotax cooling example
steps.note: Documented from EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 201 and 338-339. Use the source Rotax cooling schematic as an example, not as a claim about the GTSIO-520.

mediaPlan.rationale: A real combined-system schematic prevents the false assumption that cooling methods are always all-or-nothing.

steps.title: Airflow condition
steps.prompt: Change the qualitative inputs: low or high cooling airflow, fins clear or obstructed, baffles sealed or leaking. Observe how each condition changes the intended airflow path and relative cooling margin.
steps.note: Documented relationships from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 278-282. The planned output will use relative labels only; it will not calculate cylinder-head temperature or declare an engine airworthy.

mediaPlan.rationale: Learner-selected airflow and obstruction states make the role of fins and baffles causal rather than merely labelled.

steps.title: Inspection connection
steps.prompt: Cooling fins and baffles work as a system. Damaged or obstructed fins reduce heat-transfer area; missing or poor-fitting baffles let cooling air bypass the surfaces that need it. Actual acceptance limits and corrective action come from the applicable maintenance data.
steps.note: Documented general inspection relationship from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF p. 282. This is a recognition lesson, not an approval-to-service procedure.

mediaPlan.rationale: The final step connects theory to maintenance judgment while preserving the manual boundary.

lessons.parkedFor: Lesson 11 (Induction & Exhaust) - aspiration is taught once, inside that lesson.
lessons.title: Aspiration (parked draft)
lessons.objective: Compare naturally aspirated, mechanically supercharged and exhaust-driven turbocharged induction, explain why altitude reduces the charge available to a naturally aspirated engine, and trace the GTSIO-520 turbocharger/intercooler induction path.
lessons.completionCriteria: Trace air through each aspiration method, identify what drives the compressor where present, explain critical altitude in qualitative terms, and use the GTSIO-520 manual diagram to identify its turbocharger and induction path.

steps.title: Filling the cylinder
steps.prompt: A cylinder can only burn the oxygen charge that reaches it. As altitude increases and ambient pressure falls, predict what happens to the mass of air drawn into a naturally aspirated cylinder of fixed volume.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-142 and glossary p. 476, supported by EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 205-216.

mediaPlan.rationale: The prediction establishes the altitude problem before introducing compressors.

steps.title: Natural aspiration
steps.prompt: A naturally aspirated engine has no supercharger or turbocharger. Ambient pressure supplies the pressure difference that fills the cylinders, so available charge mass and manifold pressure decrease as the aircraft climbs, all else equal.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF glossary p. 476 and induction-system discussion pp. 133-134. This statement is qualitative and does not assign a universal power-loss rate.

mediaPlan.rationale: The baseline system has no additional mechanism to animate.

steps.title: Driven supercharger
steps.prompt: Trace the mechanically driven supercharger from crankshaft drive to compressor impeller and intake manifold. The compressor increases charge density, but the engine must supply the drive power.
steps.alt: FAA internally driven supercharger induction diagram
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-135. Use FAA Figure 3-10 as the primary visual source.

mediaPlan.rationale: The source schematic already shows the drive and induction path accurately.

steps.title: Turbo energy path
steps.prompt: Open and close the wastegate control, then trace exhaust energy through the turbine and compressor. Observe how compressor discharge, upper-deck pressure and manifold pressure are related without treating them as identical at every operating condition.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 135-142. The animation will explain control relationships qualitatively; it will not calculate boost for a real engine.

mediaPlan.rationale: A turbocharger links exhaust flow, turbine speed, compressor delivery and wastegate position; learner-controlled animation reveals that causal chain.

steps.title: Normalize or boost
steps.prompt: A normalizing turbocharger compensates for pressure loss with altitude up to its critical altitude. A ground-boosted system can raise manifold pressure above standard sea-level ambient pressure. Both descriptions depend on the installed system and its limits.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 137-140. The lesson keeps these terms distinct and does not assume every turbocharged engine is ground boosted.

mediaPlan.rationale: A concise contrast prevents the common assumption that all turbocharging has the same purpose.

steps.title: GTSIO induction
steps.prompt: Use the GTSIO-520 induction diagram to locate the turbocharger, air throttle, ducting and intercooler path. Trace air through the actual reference-engine arrangement before returning to the generic comparison.
steps.credit: Continental GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, Figure C-2-2
steps.note: Documented from the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual, PDF pp. 13, 15, 18 and 144/161 as applicable to the variant section. Confirm the exact H-variant figure and effectivity before publication.

mediaPlan.rationale: The manufacturer diagram is required for configuration-specific routing, but the exact H-variant applicability must be verified before use.
mediaPlan.assetBrief: Select the applicable GTSIO-520-H induction-system figure, preserve callouts, and add no route that the manual does not show.

steps.title: Altitude compare
steps.prompt: Move the altitude slider and switch among naturally aspirated, normalizing turbocharged and ground-boosted modes. Compare ambient pressure with a schematic manifold-pressure capability and identify the point beyond which the selected system can no longer maintain its target.
steps.note: Documented relationships from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 133-142, and EASA Module 16, PDF pp. 205-216. The graph will use normalized, explicitly schematic values unless a separately validated engine model is approved.

mediaPlan.rationale: Altitude and critical-altitude relationships are easiest to understand by changing one input and watching three system responses on the same axes.

steps.title: Limits and control
steps.prompt: Compressing the intake charge raises pressure and temperature and introduces control limits. Wastegate/controller behaviour, manifold pressure, upper-deck pressure and temperature limits must be interpreted from the installed engine and aircraft data. Rapid throttle movement and overboost are operational concerns, not effects to improvise from a generic animation.
steps.note: Documented from FAA-H-8083-32B (2023), PDF pp. 138-142, and supported by the GTSIO-520 manufacturer manual. This lesson explains system purpose but does not provide operating limits or procedures.

mediaPlan.rationale: The applicability and safety boundary should remain direct text.

checks.question: Put the four strokes in operating order.
checks.hint: Begin with the stroke that admits the fresh charge.
checks.rationale: A four-stroke cycle repeats intake, compression, power and exhaust over two crankshaft revolutions.

checks.question: What initiates combustion in the diesel cycle described by the FAA and EASA sources?
checks.hint: Consider what happens to air temperature during high compression.
answers: An electric spark across a plug gap
High temperature produced by compressing air before fuel injection
A continuously burning flame in the exhaust
checks.rationale: The cylinder compresses air to high pressure and temperature, then injected fuel ignites in that hot compressed air.

checks.question: Which description identifies a radial engine arrangement?
checks.hint: Think about the view from the propeller end.
answers: One straight cylinder bank
Two banks directly opposite each other
One or more rows of cylinders around a central crankcase
checks.rationale: A radial engine arranges its cylinders in one or more rows around a central crankcase.

checks.question: How does the GTSIO-520 overhaul manual describe the basic engine's cylinder arrangement?
checks.hint: The two banks face each other across the crankcase.
answers: Six-cylinder horizontally opposed
Nine-cylinder radial
Twelve-cylinder V-type
checks.rationale: The manual describes the basic GTSIO-520 engine as a six-cylinder horizontally opposed engine.

checks.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes spark ignition from compression ignition?
checks.hint: Focus on what starts combustion, not the number of strokes.
answers: Spark ignition uses an electric spark; compression ignition relies on the temperature of highly compressed air
Spark ignition is always two-stroke; compression ignition is always four-stroke
Spark ignition uses a turbocharger; compression ignition cannot
checks.rationale: The ignition methods differ in the combustion trigger. Stroke cycle and aspiration are separate classifications.

checks.question: Where should a technician obtain the correct ignition timing value for a particular engine?
checks.hint: A general handbook explains the principle but not every engine's approved setting.
answers: From the colour of the lesson animation
From the applicable manufacturer's technical data
From the timing used by any engine with the same number of cylinders
checks.rationale: The FAA handbook explicitly directs technicians to the engine manufacturer's recommendation.

checks.question: Put the air-cooled heat-transfer path in order.
checks.hint: Begin inside the cylinder structure and end in the atmosphere.
checks.rationale: Fins increase surface area so heat in the cylinder metal can transfer to cooling air and then to the atmosphere.

checks.question: Why are baffles important in an air-cooled engine installation?
checks.hint: Cooling air must pass across the surfaces that need it.
answers: They direct cooling air across the cylinders and fins
They ignite the fuel-air mixture
They drive the coolant pump
checks.rationale: Baffles control the airflow path so air does useful cooling work instead of bypassing the finned surfaces.

checks.question: What drives a turbocharger compressor?
checks.hint: Follow the energy path on the exhaust side.
answers: A turbine driven by exhaust gas
The magneto distributor
The radiator coolant pump
checks.rationale: Exhaust gas drives the turbine, which shares a shaft with the intake compressor.

checks.question: What is the primary purpose of a normalizing turbocharger system?
checks.hint: Compare pressure capability as the aircraft climbs.
answers: Compensate for induction-pressure loss with altitude up to a critical altitude
Convert a four-stroke engine into a two-stroke engine
Replace the engine's cooling fins
checks.rationale: A normalizing system maintains a target pressure as ambient pressure falls, until the system reaches its critical altitude.

checks.question: Put the four processes of the ideal Otto cycle in order.
checks.hint: Start with the piston moving toward top dead centre.
checks.rationale: The ideal Otto cycle compresses the charge, adds heat at constant volume, expands it, then rejects heat at constant volume.

checks.question: How does heat addition in the ideal Diesel cycle differ from the ideal Otto cycle?
checks.hint: Compare the heat-addition line on the two diagrams.
answers: Diesel adds heat at constant pressure; Otto adds it at constant volume
Diesel adds no heat; Otto adds heat with a spark
Both add heat at constant volume, but Diesel does it more slowly
checks.rationale: Fuel burns as it is injected in the diesel cycle, so heat is added at roughly constant pressure; the ideal Otto cycle adds it instantly at constant volume.

checks.question: What is valve overlap?
checks.hint: Look for the shaded interval around TDC on the timing chart.
answers: Both valves off their seats at the same time around TDC, between the exhaust and intake strokes
The intake valve staying open throughout the compression stroke
The time a valve takes to open fully
checks.rationale: The intake valve opens before TDC (lead) and the exhaust valve closes after TDC (lag), so both are open briefly, which aids cooling, charging and scavenging.

checks.question: The intake valve opening before TDC on the exhaust stroke is called:
checks.hint: The valve acts before the piston reaches the end of the stroke.
answers: Valve lead
Valve lag
Valve clearance
checks.rationale: Opening a valve before its stroke begins is valve lead; closing it after its stroke ends is valve lag.

checks.question: Why is the practical pressure-volume diagram rounder than the ideal Otto diagram?
checks.hint: Think about what the ideal cycle assumes happens instantly.
answers: Burning takes time and the valves open early and close late
A real engine has no compression stroke
The piston stops for a moment at TDC in a real engine
checks.rationale: The ideal cycle assumes instant heat addition and instant valve action; real burning and valve events take crank angle, and heat is lost to the walls.

checks.question: How many crankshaft revolutions does a two-stroke engine need to complete one operating cycle?
checks.hint: Compare it with the 720 degrees of a four-stroke cycle.
answers: One
Two
Four
checks.rationale: A two-stroke engine needs one upstroke and one downstroke, so it completes the cycle in one revolution.

checks.question: In a two-stroke cycle, which functions are accomplished during the same stroke?
checks.hint: Think about the ports that open near the bottom of the stroke.
answers: Intake and exhaust
Compression and ignition
Power and compression
checks.rationale: The intake and exhaust functions are accomplished during the same stroke, which is how one revolution is enough.

checks.question: What is at the heart of a rotary (Wankel) engine?
checks.hint: There are no reciprocating pistons.
answers: A three-sided rotor turning inside an elliptical housing
A double-acting piston in a long cylinder
A rotating cylinder block around a fixed crankshaft
checks.rationale: The rotary cycle uses a three-sided rotor in an elliptical housing; the events occur in the chambers between rotor and housing.

checks.question: Which statement best describes the crankcase?
checks.hint: Think about what has to stay aligned and what the cylinders bolt to.
answers: The rigid foundation that holds the crankshaft bearings, supports the cylinders and provides mounting for the powerplant
The chamber in which fuel and air are burned
The part that meters fuel to each cylinder
checks.rationale: The crankcase contains the bearings and supports in which the crankshaft revolves, supports the cylinder assemblies and the mounting lugs, and must stay rigid to prevent misalignment.

checks.question: What are the three main parts of a crankshaft?
checks.hint: Two cheeks and one of these make a throw.
answers: Journal, crankpin and crank cheek
Piston, ring and pin
Main bearing, cap and bolt
checks.rationale: Every crankshaft has journals that turn in the main bearings, crankpins to which the rods attach, and crank cheeks joining them.

checks.question: Which connecting-rod type is used in inline and opposed engines?
checks.hint: It has a cap and a two-piece bearing at the crankpin end.
answers: Plain
Master-and-articulated
Fork-and-blade
checks.rationale: Plain-type rods suit inline and opposed engines; master-and-articulated rods are used in radials and fork-and-blade rods mainly in V-type engines.

checks.question: What do oil control rings do?
checks.hint: Compression rings deal with gas; these deal with the other fluid.
answers: Scrape surplus oil from the cylinder wall and return it to the crankcase
Seal combustion gas above the piston crown
Hold the piston pin in place
checks.rationale: Compression rings seal the combustion gases; oil control rings limit oil reaching the combustion chamber and return the surplus to the crankcase.

checks.question: How is the aluminium cylinder head joined to the steel barrel?
checks.hint: Temperature is doing the work.
answers: The head is heated and screwed onto the chilled barrel, forming a gastight shrink joint
The two are welded along the cooling fins
They are bolted together with a gasket between them
checks.rationale: The head is expanded by heating and screwed onto the chilled barrel; as they equalise the joint becomes gastight.

checks.question: Which bearing type carries both radial and thrust loads?
checks.hint: Think of the bearing that holds propeller thrust.
answers: Deep-groove ball bearing
Straight roller bearing
Plain bushing
checks.rationale: A deep-groove ball bearing controls both radial and thrust loads; a straight roller bearing carries radial load only.

checks.question: How does the GTSIO-520-H drive its propeller?
checks.hint: The manual describes a quill shaft.
answers: Through a quill shaft and reduction gear to a flanged propeller shaft
Directly from a flange formed on the crankshaft
Through a belt drive
checks.rationale: The crankshaft's internal spline mates with a quill shaft that drives the reduction gear, which drives the flanged propeller shaft; a direct-drive engine such as the IO-520 has the propeller flange on the crankshaft itself.

checks.question: Put these in the order force passes through them during the power stroke.
checks.hint: Start where the expanding gas meets the engine and finish at the shaft that turns.
items: Expanding gas pushes on the piston
The piston pin passes the load to the connecting rod
The connecting rod turns the crankpin
The crankshaft rotates and drives the propeller shaft
checks.rationale: Gas pressure on the piston is carried through the pin and rod to the crankpin, and the crankshaft turns the reciprocating force into rotation that drives the propeller.
